newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Suharto's eldest son in limelight after gold deal.
newsitem.headline: Suharto's eldest son in limelight after gold deal.

text.p: Long in the shadows of his more flamboyant siblings, Indonesian President Suharto's eldest son of stepped into the limelight this week after a sweetheart deal with the company controlling a massive gold find.

Sigit Harjojudanto's Panutan Duta group signed a deal with Bre-X Minerals Ltd of Canada to act as a consultant for the Alberta-based firm's Busang gold field in the Indonesian province of East Kalimantan on the island of Borneo, which has estimated gold reserves of at least 47 million ounces.

Under the agreement, Sigit's company will receive $40 million over 40 months and a 10 percent interest in two of the richest Busang fields subject to helping Bre-X receive essential permits from the Indonesian government, the Canadian firm has said.
Political analysts in Jakarta were hesitant to comment on the record about the deal, but privately said Bre-X's problems with another Indonesian partner now appear close to a solution.

Indonesian businessman Jusuf Merukh has said he has a 20 percent claim on Busang and an option for an additional 20 percent. Merukh said on Tuesday he would continue to pursue his claim for a total 40 percent stake.

The Indonesian government has so far refused to grant Bre-X contracts for work needed to further explore and develop the two richest sections of the property, and has said it will not do so until the dispute is resolved.
"Merukh's role is now probably over," said one political analyst. "He has been close to the government in the past, but maybe he's fallen out of favour."
Other analysts said it was not surprising that Bre-X should choose a company linked to the Suharto family as its consultant, but added that Sigit was not considered very active in business.
A source close to the first family said Sigit, 45, was "perhaps a bit of an introvert".
"He doesn't speak much, he's very much a family man," the source said. "He's a keen golfer."
In contrast, Sigit's younger brothers Bambang Trihatmodjo and Hutomo Mandala Putra, also known as Tommy, control highly visible businesses.

Bambang is the head of the conglomerate Bimantara Citra Tommy is the sole beneficiary of a controversial national car policy that gives his Timor Putra Nasional company tax and tariff breaks to build a national car in partnership with Kia Motors of South Korea.
Their elder sister, Siti Hardianti Rukmana, is the head of toll road operator Citra Marga, while another two Suharto daughters own smaller businesses.
"Sigit is certainly the least well known of all the Suharto sons," said a Western diplomat in Jakarta. "This is going to be his first high-profile project."
Still, Sigit has not been entirely unknown. He was associated with a national lottery that was banned in 1993 after protests by Moslem leaders that it promoted gambling.

His eldest son, Ari Sigit, attracted attention earlier this year when one of his companies tried to impose a levy on beer sales on the resort island of Bali. A law permitting the move was later withdrawn.

Newspapers have said Sigit's business interests include a portion of Tommy's Humpuss group, a significant holding in unlisted Bank Central Asia and a stake in PT PENI, a petrochemicals joint venture with British Petroleum
